name: style-economist
title: Economist house style
description:
The house style of The Economist, as something a document can be measured against. Choose this profile if you want prose that is concrete and active, Anglo-Saxon in preference to Latinate, and around twenty words to a sentence. A finding means the document sits outside that register, which is a statement about fit and not a defect.

Nine rules, most of them two-sided bands, derived from the paper's own published guide - Orwell's six rules, 'short words Use them. They are often Anglo-Saxon rather than Latin in origin', 'full stops Use plenty. They keep sentences short', 'dashes ... ideally not more than one pair per paragraph', 'Do not be too didactic' - and from the paper's July 2026 study of 55,940 sentences, whose findings are almost all rates of the same kind. Every rule is off by default and reports a rate over the whole document. Crossing a band is a statement about fit with one register and nothing else. The thresholds are the first thing you would change: see corpus below for what each one was calibrated against, and note that four of the twelve edges have no contact with any corpus outside the register sample and say so in their own measured field.

corpus.note: Two references, and they carry different weight. (1) The local sanity check: 16 documents / 19,555 words of human technical documentation under /home/bas/Downloads, being every document of 250 words or more that clears the engine's default prose gate. That corpus is a different register on purpose - it says whether a band is on the right scale, never where the register sits. (2) The register sample: 3,251 words of continuous prose lifted from the style guide itself (its introduction and its longer entries - metaphors, jargon, unnecessary words, sloppy writing, short words). That is prose written and edited to this house style, which is the closest reachable thing to a reference corpus; economist.com refuses automated requests, so no sample of the paper's actual journalism could be measured. It is a small sample, it is instructional rather than analytical in register, and where the guide quotes poor prose as an example the counts are contaminated - that is exactly why a passive-voice rule was left out. Register-sample rates per 1000 words: comma 61.2, semicolon-or-parenthesis 29.8, sentence endings 44.9 (22.3 words a sentence), long words 16.3, nominalisations 34.1, intensifiers 1.8, didactic openers 0.0, sentence-length variation cv 1.16. An earlier draft measured 18 documents / 24,527 words by widening the prose gate to 200 words a sentence; the two extra documents were a Python source file and a README of headings and list items, and between them they supplied five findings, including the only corpus contact the comma ceiling had. The gate is back at the engine default. Retune all of it against prose you actually want to sound like.

voice: Third person, active, concrete. Sentences of about twenty words with short ones landing among them. Commas and brackets doing structural work rather than decoration. Anglo-Saxon words in preference to Latinate ones, and a plain declarative in preference to an emphatic adverb.
note: Twelve rules, eight of them the two sides of a band and four of them one-sided ceilings where a floor would be meaningless - no document is off this register for containing too few long words, nominalisations, intensifiers or em dashes. Eight edges are calibrated against the local corpus and fire on between 1 and 4 of its 16 documents; four have no local corpus contact and label themselves as such in `measured`: the short-sentence edge, the comma ceiling, the intensifier ceiling and the didactic-opener ceiling. The one genuine gap is semicolon-paren, which has a floor and no ceiling; its note says what closing the band would need. All twelve rules run at the engine's default prose gate rather than a widened one, because a rate over a code listing or a page of list items is a number about markup: every test document in the set clears that gate, and the two documents it excludes from the local corpus are a Python source file and a README of headings. Composition with the detection sets already in this repository is by construction: this profile's comma floor (30) sits above candidates/economist.json comma-scarcity (20), its nominalisation ceiling (55) below nominalisation-pileup (70), its em-dash ceiling (25) below em-dash-density (35), and its even-rhythm edge (0.60) above humanizer-de uniform-sentence-length (0.40). In each pair the outer number belongs to the detection rule and the inner one to this band, so a document between them is off this register and nothing more, and a document past both gets two findings that agree. Three disagreements do not nest and are declared in `tension`. Note also what this profile does not have: no floor under the em-dash rate, because requiring em dashes would contradict rules/em-dash.json outright rather than merely disagree with it.

tension.note: That set reports every em dash as a house-style matter, and it is selected in this repository's own configuration. This register permits paired dashes, sparingly: the guide's own instruction is 'not more than one pair per sentence, ideally not more than one pair per paragraph', which is roughly the 25 per 1000 words this profile uses as its ceiling. The two verdicts are independent and both stand. If you disagree with the em-dash rule for your own writing, put it in the ignore list of your own configuration file, under your name, in review.

humanizer-de reports sentence-length variation at or below cv 0.40. This profile's even-rhythm edge is 0.60. Between 0.40 and 0.60 only this profile reports anything, and what it reports is that the prose is flatter than this register runs, which is a fit judgement. At or below 0.40 both report, and they agree.

candidates/humanizer-de.json reports six or more paired dash asides per 1000 words. This profile permits up to 25 em dashes per 1000, and the guide's instruction is that they come in pairs - 'not more than one pair per sentence' - so a document sitting just inside this ceiling carries about twelve pairs per 1000 words, twice what that rule reports. This is the sharpest disagreement in the repository: the paired aside that The Economist's guide teaches is the same construction humanizer-de counts as a cluster pattern. Both verdicts stand and neither is a claim about authorship. If you are writing to this register, ignore paired-dash-aside in your own configuration file, under your name, in review.

rules.name: Sentence length outside the range this register keeps
rules.description: Sentence endings per 1000 words, which is average sentence length turned upside down. Below the band the reader goes a long way between full stops; above it the prose is staccato, which this register uses for a paragraph but not for a page.
rules.suggest: Outside the economist band (30 to 80 sentence endings per 1000 words, or about 12 to 33 words a sentence). Below it, break the longest sentences in two; the guide's entry for full stops reads in full 'Use plenty. They keep sentences short. This helps the reader.' Above it, let some of these clauses join up; a short sentence works here because it lands after a long one.
rules.note: A measurement of fit, not a defect: a great deal of excellent prose runs longer than 33 words a sentence, and plenty of good reporting is written entirely in short ones. Read the document before you read the number. A page of headings, list items and table rows carries few full stops and will land below the band without holding a single long sentence. This rule counts full stops, not sentences, so a document made mostly of headings, list items and table cells reads as one very long sentence. The engine's prose gate stops the extreme cases - a document averaging more than 60 words between full stops is not measured at all - but a mixed document, prose paragraphs above a table, can still land here on the strength of its fragments. Where the badge disagrees with the page, the page is right. Selecting this profile is the statement that you want this register, so the fix is an instruction, not a question. If the band is wrong for this document, move it with `tune` in slop.json or drop the profile; do not leave the finding unaddressed on the grounds that the register is a choice.
rules.measured: band 30-80 endings /1000. Register sample (3,251 words of the guide's own prose) 44.9. Local human technical corpus, 16 documents / 19,555 words that clear the engine's default prose gate, ran 17.3 min / 20.1 p10 / 31.4 p25 / 45.5 median / 66.8 p90 / 75.0 max. The low edge is set from the register sample at about two-thirds of it, which places it just below the local p25; it reports 4 of the 16. An earlier draft measured 18 documents / 24,527 words with the prose gate widened to 200 words a sentence, and 2 of the 6 documents it reported were a Python source file and a README of headings and list items, neither of which has sentences to be long. The gate is back at the engine default, which is what excludes them.  Upper edge: band 30-80 endings /1000. Register sample 44.9. Local corpus of 16 documents ran 17.3 min / 45.5 median / 75.0 max, so no local document reaches this edge and it reports 0 of 16. This edge has no local corpus contact: it is the register sample at roughly 1.8x, set above the local maximum, and no corpus in the target register was reachable to check it. Retune it first. Its hit fixture measures 5.7 words a sentence, which clears the prose gate's four-word floor with little to spare, so prose more clipped than that is not measured at all rather than reported.

hit: The argument over the new berths at the eastern end of the harbour has been running for three years now, and it has acquired the particular quality of exhaustion that attaches to disputes in which every participant has already said everything he intends to say and none of them is willing to be the first to stop repeating it. On one side stand the terminal operators, who point out that the boxes are stacked six high on a quay designed for four and that a berth which is not begun this spring cannot be finished before the end of the decade, by which time the traffic will either have found another port or have been turned away for so long that it will not come back at all. On the other stand the provincial authorities, who observe that the same operators made the same argument in the boom before the last one and then spent the following six years asking to be released from the lease payments on the cranes they had insisted were indispensable. Between them sit the unions, whose position has the merit of being consistent, which is that nothing whatever should be built, agreed, leased or dredged until the wage round has been settled on terms that the men on the night shift are prepared to accept without another ballot. The provincial authorities have commissioned two studies, the first of which concluded that demand would hold and the second of which concluded that it would not, and both of which cost rather more than the berths would have cost had anybody simply built them in the year the first study was ordered. It is worth saying that the studies were not badly done, and that the disagreement between them reflects a genuine disagreement about how long shipping lines will keep sailing around the Cape rather than any failure of arithmetic on the part of the consultants who produced them. What has changed in the past six months is that the Egyptians have begun offering discounts steep enough to tempt the smaller lines back through the canal, which suggests that the rerouting may unwind faster than either study assumed and that the pessimists on the provincial side may turn out to have been right for reasons they never actually advanced. None of this has altered anybody's position by so much as a metre of quay, because the positions were never really about the forecasts in the first place and were always about who would carry the loss if the forecasts turned out to be wrong. That question has an answer, and everybody in the room knows what it is, which is why nobody in the room will say it aloud. The operators will carry the loss on the cranes, the province will carry the loss on the land, and the unions will carry the loss in jobs that are never created and therefore never appear in any statistic that anybody has to explain to a committee. Somebody will eventually decide, and the decision will be taken in a fortnight by people who have not read either study, on the basis of a summary written by an official who has read only the second one. That is not a scandal and it is not even unusual, but it is worth remembering the next time somebody proposes commissioning a third.

The port is busy. Traffic rose a tenth last year. The operators are turning ships away. This is new. For a decade they complained about spare capacity. Now they complain about the lack of it. The mood on the quay has changed. Dockers work double shifts. The cranes run past midnight. Boxes stack six high. The yard was built for four. Something has to give. The surge is not about European industry. It is about the Red Sea. Ships now sail around the Cape. That adds ten days to a voyage from Shanghai. Cargo has moved north as a result. Rotterdam has taken most of it. Antwerp has taken some. Hamburg has taken the rest. None of the three trusts the boom. All three are drawing up plans anyway. The plans involve concrete. The concrete involves money. The money involves the province. The province wants to wait. The operators want to build. The unions want a wage round first. Nobody has moved. Cairo has moved. The canal authority has cut its tolls. Smaller lines are already going back. The big lines are watching. If they follow the boom ends. If they do not it continues. Nobody knows which. The studies disagree. The consultants disagree. The ministers have not read either study. A decision is due in a fortnight. It will be made on a summary. The summary runs to two pages. One of them is a chart. The chart shows two lines. They cross in 2029. That is the whole argument. It will be settled by a chart. Somebody drew that chart in an afternoon. Nobody will ever check it. The berths will be built or they will not. The quay will be full or it will be empty. Either way the dockers will work nights.
miss: The port has never been busier. Traffic through Rotterdam rose by a tenth last year, and the terminal operators, who spent most of the previous decade grumbling that Europe had built far too much capacity, now find themselves turning ships away at the mouth of the Maas. That is a pleasant problem. It is also a temporary one, for the surge owes less to any revival of European industry than to the rerouting of Asian cargo away from the Red Sea, and a rerouting can be undone as fast as it was made. Ask the Egyptians. Canal revenues in Cairo have roughly halved since the shipping lines began the long haul around the Cape, and the finance ministry has quietly stopped citing them in its budget documents (the canal authority disputes the figure, though it has yet to publish a better one). Dockers (who have watched three such booms) know this. They have seen the cycle before; the men who load the boxes at midnight are markedly less excited by the annual figures than the consultants who write them up. Rotterdam is not alone. Antwerp, Hamburg and Piraeus all report the same swell, and all three have begun the same argument about whether to pour concrete for berths that may stand idle by the end of the decade, an argument that turns, as such arguments always do, on how long a rerouting lasts. Nobody knows. The Dutch government, which owns much of the land, would rather wait; the operators, who own the cranes, would rather build; and the unions, who own the labour, would rather neither side moved at all until the wage round is settled. Something will give. What gives first will probably be the argument itself, because the ships are already coming and the boxes are already stacked six high on the quay, and a berth that is not built this year is a berth that is not available for the next five. The concrete will be poured. It usually is.

rules.name: Sentence-length variation outside the range this register keeps
rules.description: Sentence-length variation, as standard deviation over mean. Below the band the sentences are close to a single length; above it the rhythm swings hard between the very short and the very long.
rules.suggest: Outside the economist band (variation 0.60 to 1.45). Below it, cut one long sentence in half and let a short one land after it - the guide quotes Mark Twain on the writer who 'at times may indulge himself with a long one'. Above it, even out the extremes - the guide's image is a torch-light procession rather than a sea-serpent with half its arches under the water.
rules.note: A judgement about fit rather than about quality: prose that runs flat is correct and readable, and some registers want exactly the swing this one does not. Selecting this profile is the statement that you want this register, so the fix is an instruction, not a question. If the band is wrong for this document, move it with `tune` in slop.json or drop the profile; do not leave the finding unaddressed on the grounds that the register is a choice.
rules.measured: band cv 0.60-1.45. Register sample 1.16. Local corpus of 16 documents ran 0.49 min / 0.70 p10 / 0.82 median / 1.30 p90 / 1.54 max; the low edge is the local p10 rounded down and reports 1 of 16. humanizer-de reports the same measurement at or below 0.40, so this edge sits outside it by design.  Upper edge: band cv 0.60-1.45. Register sample 1.16. Local corpus of 16 documents ran 0.49 min / 0.82 median / 1.30 p90 / 1.54 max; the high edge sits between the local p90 and the local maximum and reports 1 of 16. An earlier draft put the local maximum at 1.98 and the p90 at 1.48, but that maximum was a Python source file admitted by a widened prose gate; with the gate at its default the file is not measured and the edge is unchanged.

hit: The harbour authority published its annual traffic figures on Tuesday morning. Container volumes rose by nine per cent over the course of the year. The provincial government has asked for a reconciliation before the summer recess. That request has been made twice before and has been ignored on both occasions. Traffic through the western terminal fell by two per cent over the same period. Managers there blame the loss on a scheduling change made by a single line. The line moved its weekly Asian service to Antwerp in the autumn. It has since moved a second service, though not the first, back again. Nobody at either terminal will say what was offered to secure the return. Wage talks for the night shift opened in March and remain unresolved. The union is asking for a rise of six per cent across three years. The employers have offered four per cent and a review clause after eighteen months. A ballot on that offer is expected before the end of next month. Most people on the quay expect the offer to be rejected the first time. Dredging at the fourth berth is now scheduled to resume in the autumn. The contractor has warned that its vessel may not be available in October. A second contractor has been approached but has not yet quoted a price. The authority expects to award the work before the end of the year. Nobody on the quay believes that the work will begin before the spring.

The berth is closed. Nobody says why. The dredger left in March. It has not come back. The crane sits idle. Traffic is down. Managers blame the schedule. The union blames the province. The province blames the weather. Nothing moves. Not the dredger. Not the talks. Not the boxes. What is actually happening, and it has taken three months and two leaked memoranda for anybody outside the harbour authority to work it out, is that the survey commissioned before the dredging began found a layer of contaminated silt across the whole eastern approach, and that the disposal licence required to move that silt anywhere at all was never applied for, because the official responsible for applying for it retired in January and nobody was appointed to replace him until the middle of April, by which time the dredger's charter had expired and the vessel had been contracted to a project in the Baltic that will not release her until the autumn. That is the story. Nobody will confirm it. Everybody repeats it. Somebody will be blamed. It will not be the official who retired. The dredger is still in the Baltic. The grant window is still shut. The silt is still there.

rules.name: Commas outside the rate this register uses
rules.description: Commas per 1000 words. Below the band the prose is mostly bare declaratives carrying little subordination; above it the sentences hold more subordinate material than this register asks a reader to carry at once.
rules.suggest: Outside the economist band (30 to 85 commas per 1000 words). Below it, subordinate a clause or two. Above it, split some of the longer sentences. The guide's instruction runs 'Use commas as an aid to understanding. Too many in one sentence can be confusing.'
rules.note: A measurement of fit, not a defect: plenty of good writing sits below the band deliberately, and above it the subordination may be doing real work. Selecting this profile is the statement that you want this register, so the fix is an instruction, not a question. If the band is wrong for this document, move it with `tune` in slop.json or drop the profile; do not leave the finding unaddressed on the grounds that the register is a choice.

Upper edge: ceiling 85 /1000, and one of the four edges in this profile with no local corpus contact. Register sample 61.2. Local corpus of 16 documents ran 41.5 median / 69.6 p90 / 79.1 max, so the edge sits above the local maximum and reports 0 of 16. An earlier draft reported 1 of 18 here, but that document was a Python source file whose commas were argument separators, admitted by a widened prose gate; it is the reason the gate is back at the engine default. The edge is the register sample at about 1.4x and the local corpus cannot check it.

rules.name: Fewer semicolons and brackets than this register uses
rules.description: Semicolons and round brackets per 1000 words, counted together as the punctuation that holds a second thought inside one sentence. Each bracket counts, so a pair counts twice. Below the floor the document has almost no aside and every thought arrives in its own sentence.
rules.suggest: Below the economist floor (15 semicolons or brackets per 1000 words). Let one aside go in brackets and one pause take a semicolon - the guide asks for a semicolon to 'mark a pause longer than a comma and shorter than a full stop'.
rules.note: This register expects them, and there is no upper edge here: that is a gap rather than a permission, and the reason is below. A fit judgement, not a defect. One-sided, and the gap is real. The floor is calibrated; there is no ceiling, so a document can carry any number of brackets and semicolons and this profile will say nothing. The local corpus shows how far that reaches: its median is 65.6 per 1000 and its maximum 110.3, both well above the register sample's 29.8, because technical documentation brackets units, aliases and function names. A ceiling was not shipped because the only in-register measurement available is a single number from a 3,251-word sample, and the guide's own high-side guidance ('Don't overdo them') is about one sentence, which a document rate cannot see. Closing the band needs a rate measured over real journalism in this register; until then, read silence here as unmeasured rather than as on-target. Selecting this profile is the statement that you want this register, so the fix is an instruction, not a question. If the band is wrong for this document, move it with `tune` in slop.json or drop the profile; do not leave the finding unaddressed on the grounds that the register is a choice.
rules.measured: floor 15 /1000, no ceiling. Register sample 29.8. Local corpus of 16 documents ran 1.7 min / 21.9 p10 / 31.9 p25 / 65.6 median / 108.0 p90 / 110.3 max - technical documentation is bracket-rich, which is why the local median sits at more than twice the register sample. The floor is set below the local p10 and reports 1 of 16. The pattern counts each bracket, so one pair of them counts twice; the register sample's 29.8 is about fifteen pairs per 1000 words. This is the one rule in the profile with a floor and no ceiling, which is a known gap rather than a finding: see its note.

rules.name: More em dashes than this register uses
rules.description: Em dashes per 1000 words. This register uses them in pairs and rations them, and above the ceiling the dash is doing work that commas, colons and full stops would otherwise divide between them.

rules.note: The guide asks for “not more than one pair per sentence, ideally not more than one pair per paragraph”, which at this register's sentence length works out near 22 per 1000 words. This says nothing about who wrote the document. It is a rate, and this register's rate is lower. The em dash is not evidence of anything about authorship, and three separate measurements recorded in this repository's research log agree on that. This rule is a register rate and only that.
